newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian gilt prices leap on low interest hopes.
newsitem.headline: Indian gilt prices leap on low interest hopes.

text.p: Indian securities prices rose sharply in active trade on Thursday as market players went on a buying spree in anticipation of a fall in interest rates, dealers said.
They said a variety of factors including low call money rates, revised central selling bank prices and expectataions of a fall in terest rates triggered frenzied buying.
Call money ended Thursday at 0.10-0.25 percent, down from opening quotes of 0.75-1.50 percent and money market dealers said there were few borrowers in a market flush with funds.
Dealers said liquidity with the banking system, which has been good in recent times, has been boosted by central bank dollar purchases and a surge in foreign exchange reserves.
India's foreign currency reserves stood at an all-time high of $21.16 billion on March 21.
"Foreign currency assets with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) increased by $1.46 billion just between February 28 and March 21," said a dealer.
"This has injected more than 52 billion rupees into the banking system," he said.
"Typically when call is easy, trade in securities tends to pick up," said another dealer.
"Trades today were worth 4.73 billion rupees against Wednesday's 3.54 billion," he said.
"RBI's revised price-list which took effect today also indicated to the market that interest rates are headed south," the dealer added.
The RBI revised prices of several securities upwards in its selling list effective April 3.
"This is a clear sign they want to push yields down," the dealer said.
He said investments in securities would increase in such conditions as banks' portfolios would appreciate in a falling interest rate scenario.
"Even foreign banks, who normally prefer short to medium-maturity stocks are picking up long-dated securities," he added.
Dealers said yield on treasury bills also fell as buying interest drove prices up.
The July 4 treasury bill yielded 7.75 percent against its last 8.35 while the July 18 bill traded at 8.05 percent against 8.60 percent, dealers said.
December-maturity treasury bills yielded 9.50 percent,
Market players said they expected the forthcoming credit policy to contain measures which will result in a fall in interest rates.
The RBI announces its credit policy for the first half of 1997/98 (April-March) on April 15.
